title: 12 — Observability & Operations on Azure
html:
12 — Observability & Operations on Azure

Application Insights, Log Analytics, the KQL you'll actually write, alerts that are worth waking up for, and cost control.

1. The Azure Monitor stack

flowchart TB
    subgraph Sources
      A[App Insights SDK / OpenTelemetry]
      B[Platform metrics — automatic]
      C[Resource logs — via diagnostic settings]
      D[Activity log — control-plane operations]
    end
    A --> LA[(Log Analytics workspace)]
    C --> LA
    D --> LA
    B --> MET[(Azure Monitor metrics store)]
    LA --> KQL[KQL queries · workbooks · dashboards]
    MET --> KQL
    LA --> ALR[Alert rules]
    MET --> ALR
    ALR --> AG[Action groups:<br/>email · SMS · Teams · webhook ·<br/>Logic App · PagerDuty]
Store Holds Query with Retention
Metrics Numeric time series, pre-aggregated Metrics explorer, metric alerts 93 days
Logs (Log Analytics) Structured events, traces, requests, dependencies KQL Configurable per table; Basic/Auxiliary tiers are cheaper

⚠️ Metrics are cheap, fast, and low-cardinality; logs are expensive, flexible, and high-cardinality. Alert on metrics where you can; investigate in logs.

Key setup decisions:

  • One Log Analytics workspace per environment (not per app) so you can correlate across services. Separate prod from non-prod so noisy dev data doesn't inflate the production bill or the query surface.
  • Workspace-based Application Insights — classic AI is retired 🔄.
  • Diagnostic settings on every resource to send resource logs to the workspace. This is not automatic and is routinely forgotten until an incident.

2. Application Insights

2.1 Wiring it up

// The classic SDK — still the richest experience for ASP.NET Core
builder.Services.AddApplicationInsightsTelemetry();

// ⭐ Or OpenTelemetry with the Azure Monitor exporter — vendor-neutral, and the direction of travel
builder.Services.AddOpenTelemetry()
    .ConfigureResource(r => r.AddService("shop-api", serviceVersion: version))
    .UseAzureMonitor(o => o.ConnectionString = cfg["APPLICATIONINSIGHTS_CONNECTION_STRING"])
    .WithTracing(t => t
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation(o => o.RecordException = true)
        .AddHttpClientInstrumentation()
        .AddSqlClientInstrumentation(o => o.SetDbStatementForText = true))  // ⚠️ check for PII
    .WithMetrics(m => m
        .AddAspNetCoreInstrumentation()
        .AddRuntimeInstrumentation());   // GC, thread pool, exceptions

💡 Use the connection string, not the instrumentation key — instrumentation-key-only ingestion is retired 🔄.

What you get automatically: incoming requests, outgoing HTTP and SQL dependencies (with duration and success), exceptions, performance counters, and distributed trace correlation across services via W3C trace context.

2.2 The telemetry tables

Table Contains
requests Incoming HTTP requests: name, duration, result code, success
dependencies Outgoing calls: HTTP, SQL, Service Bus, Blob — with target and duration
exceptions Stack traces, linked to the request
traces Your ILogger output
customEvents / customMetrics What you emit deliberately
availabilityResults Synthetic tests
pageViews, browserTimings Client-side (with the JS SDK)

2.3 Enriching telemetry — do this on day one

// A telemetry initialiser adds properties to EVERY item — the cheapest way to make logs queryable
public sealed class EnrichmentInitializer(IHttpContextAccessor accessor) : ITelemetryInitializer
{
    public void Initialize(ITelemetry telemetry)
    {
        var context = accessor.HttpContext;
        if (context is null) return;

        telemetry.Context.User.AuthenticatedUserId = context.User.GetObjectId();   // never email
        telemetry.Context.GlobalProperties["TenantId"] =
            context.User.FindFirst("tid")?.Value ?? "unknown";

        if (context.Request.Headers.TryGetValue("X-Correlation-Id", out var correlationId))
            telemetry.Context.GlobalProperties["CorrelationId"] = correlationId!;
    }
}
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ITelemetryInitializer, EnrichmentInitializer>();

// Structured logging — named placeholders become QUERYABLE FIELDS, not an opaque string
logger.LogInformation("Portfolio rebalanced {PortfolioId} {TradeCount} {ElapsedMs}",
    portfolioId, trades.Count, elapsed.TotalMilliseconds);

// A business metric you can alert on
telemetryClient.GetMetric("TradesApproved", "Desk").TrackValue(1, desk);

⚠️ Never log secrets, tokens, or PII. And be careful with SetDbStatementForText — parameter values may end up in your traces.

2.4 Sampling — you will need it

Adaptive sampling is on by default in the ASP.NET Core SDK, and Functions samples aggressively too. Under load, telemetry is dropped — and people are surprised when a specific request isn't there.

{
  "ApplicationInsights": {
    "EnableAdaptiveSampling": true,
    "SamplingSettings": { "MaxTelemetryItemsPerSecond": 20 }
  }
}

💡 Sampling is telemetry-item aware: it keeps a request and its related dependencies, exceptions and traces together, so a sampled-in transaction is still complete end-to-end. 💡 Exclude what you must never lose — exceptions and specific critical events — via a telemetry processor, and sample the noisy successful requests hard.

3. KQL — the queries you'll actually write

// 1. Failure rate by endpoint over 24 hours
requests
| where timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize total = count(), failed = countif(success == false) by operation_Name
| extend failureRate = round(100.0 * failed / total, 2)
| where total > 100
| order by failureRate desc

// 2. p50/p95/p99 latency trend
requests
| where timestamp > ago(7d)
| summarize p50 = percentile(duration, 50),
            p95 = percentile(duration, 95),
            p99 = percentile(duration, 99)
        by bin(timestamp, 1h), operation_Name
| render timechart

// 3. ⭐ Slowest dependency per request — "where is the time going?"
dependencies
| where timestamp > ago(1h)
| summarize count(), avgMs = avg(duration), p95 = percentile(duration, 95)
        by type, target, name
| order by p95 desc
| take 20

// 4. Everything about one request (the incident-response query)
union requests, dependencies, exceptions, traces
| where operation_Id == "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736"
| project timestamp, itemType, name, message, duration, success, resultCode
| order by timestamp asc

// 5. Top exceptions with a sample stack
exceptions
| where timestamp > ago(24h)
| summarize count(), any(details) by type, outerMessage, operation_Name
| order by count_ desc

// 6. ⚠️ N+1 detection — many identical dependency calls in one operation
dependencies
| where timestamp > ago(1h) and type == "SQL"
| summarize callCount = count(), totalMs = sum(duration) by operation_Id, name
| where callCount > 20
| order by callCount desc

// 7. Correlating a failure with a deployment
requests
| where timestamp > ago(6h)
| summarize failureRate = 100.0 * countif(success == false) / count()
        by bin(timestamp, 5m), cloud_RoleName, appVersion       // ← compare versions
| render timechart

// 8. Dependency failures by target (is it us or them?)
dependencies
| where timestamp > ago(1h) and success == false
| summarize count() by target, resultCode
| order by count_ desc

// 9. Thread-pool / GC health (with runtime instrumentation)
customMetrics
| where name in ("dotnet.thread_pool.queue.length", "dotnet.gc.pause.time")
| summarize avg(value) by name, bin(timestamp, 1m)
| render timechart

// 10. Cost: what's filling my workspace?
Usage
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| summarize GB = sum(Quantity) / 1000 by DataType
| order by GB desc

KQL essentials: where → summarize ... by → project → order by → take. bin(timestamp, 5m) buckets time. ago() and between() for ranges. extend adds computed columns. join kind=inner correlates tables. render timechart for a graph. let defines variables at the top.

💡 Save the queries your team runs during incidents as workbook cells or shared queries. At 3am, nobody writes good KQL from scratch.

4. Alerting

4.1 Alert on symptoms, not causes

❌ Alert on ✔ Alert on
CPU > 80% User-facing error rate breaching the SLO
Memory > 90% p99 latency above target
A pod/instance restarted Requests failing, or queue age growing
Disk 70% full Disk will be full in 4 hours (predictive)

Why: high CPU with happy users isn't an incident; failing users with normal CPU is. Cause-based alerts generate noise and train people to ignore pages.

4.2 Burn-rate alerting

Alerting on "error rate > 1% for 5 minutes" is either too noisy or too slow. Burn rate — how fast you're consuming the error budget — fixes it:

Severity Condition Response
Page 14.4× burn over 1h and over 5min The monthly budget is gone in ~2 days
Page 6× burn over 6h and over 30min Urgent
Ticket 3× burn over 24h Next working day
Ticket 1× burn over 3 days Track the trend

The two-window requirement (long window for significance, short window for currency) avoids both false alarms and alerts that fire after the problem resolved.

4.3 Practical setup

resource failureAlert 'Microsoft.Insights/scheduledQueryRules@2023-03-15-preview' = {
  name: 'shop-api-high-failure-rate'
  location: location
  properties: {
    severity: 1                                   // 0 critical … 4 verbose
    evaluationFrequency: 'PT5M'
    windowSize: 'PT15M'
    scopes: [appInsights.id]
    criteria: {
      allOf: [{
        query: '''
          requests
          | where success == false and client_Type != "Browser"
          | summarize failed = count()
        '''
        timeAggregation: 'Total'
        threshold: 50
        operator: 'GreaterThan'
        failingPeriods: { numberOfEvaluationPeriods: 2, minFailingPeriodsToAlert: 2 }
      }]
    }
    autoMitigate: true
    actions: { actionGroups: [onCallActionGroup.id] }
  }
}

Alerts every production service should have:

Alert Threshold
Availability / failure rate SLO burn rate
p95 or p99 latency Above your stated budget
Dependency failures Failure rate per target
Queue depth / oldest-message age Growing or above a threshold
Dead-letter count > 0
Unhandled exceptions Any new exception type
Certificate expiry ≥21 days ahead
Key Vault 403/429 Any
Database DTU/vCore % > 80% sustained
Cost anomaly Deviation from the forecast
Availability test failing From ≥2 regions

Every alert needs: a clear title naming the user impact, a runbook link, an owner, and a severity that maps to a defined response. ⚠️ Track pages per on-call shift. More than ~2 actionable pages per shift means the system or the alerting needs work; a shift full of non-actionable pages means the real one will be missed. Delete or downgrade any alert ignored three times.

4.4 Availability tests

Synthetic checks from multiple Azure regions against a real endpoint. 💡 Use a standard test hitting a health endpoint that exercises dependencies, from ≥3 locations, alerting when ≥2 fail — that avoids paging on a single flaky probe location.

5. Dashboards and workbooks

Three tiers:

  1. Service overview — one screen per service: RED metrics, error budget remaining, saturation, dependency health, deployment markers.
  2. Business overview — the handful of numbers the company cares about, so a broken funnel is visible even when infrastructure looks green.
  3. Deep-dive workbooks — per endpoint, per dependency, per queue, reached from the overview.

Design rules: the top-left panel answers "is this healthy?" in two seconds; consistent time ranges; percentiles, not averages; annotate deploys; and put the runbook link on the dashboard.

⚠️ Overlay deployment and configuration-change events on every dashboard. "What changed?" resolves a large share of incidents in the first five minutes, and it's the most neglected signal.

6. Distributed tracing across services

Trace (one user request)
├── span: POST /api/rebalance                    [420 ms]
│   ├── span: authorise                          [  3 ms]
│   ├── span: SELECT portfolio + holdings        [ 45 ms]
│   ├── span: HTTP GET pricing-service/quotes    [180 ms]  ← the cost
│   │   └── span: (in pricing) SELECT prices     [160 ms]  ← the REAL cost
│   ├── span: compute trades                     [ 30 ms]
│   └── span: INSERT trades + outbox             [ 40 ms]

W3C trace context (traceparent) propagates automatically over HTTP. ⚠️ It does not propagate across queues automatically — you must inject it into message properties and restore it on the consumer side, and that boundary is exactly where you most need the trace.

// Producer
message.ApplicationProperties["traceparent"] = Activity.Current?.Id;

// Consumer
using var activity = ActivitySource.StartActivity("ProcessTradeApproved",
    ActivityKind.Consumer, parentId: message.ApplicationProperties["traceparent"]?.ToString());

Set cloud_RoleName per service (via the resource attributes or a telemetry initialiser) so the Application Map renders your topology correctly — it's genuinely useful for spotting an unexpected dependency or a chatty call path.

7. Autoscaling and operational automation

Autoscale rules and the fast-out/slow-in principle are covered in file 06 §5. The operational additions:

Tool Use
Azure Automation runbooks Scheduled maintenance, start/stop dev environments
Logic Apps Alert → create a ticket, post to Teams, call an API
Action group webhooks Route to PagerDuty/Opsgenie
Azure Advisor Automated recommendations for cost, reliability, security, performance
Service Health alerts ⭐ Set these up. Azure will have incidents; you want to know it's them, not you

💡 A Service Health alert on your subscription's regions and services is five minutes of setup that saves an hour of misdirected investigation during a platform incident.

8. Cost control for observability itself

⚠️ Log Analytics and Application Insights ingestion is frequently a top-3 line item and it creeps silently.

Lever Effect
Sampling The biggest lever. 20 items/sec adaptive is a sane default
Per-table retention Keep requests for 90 days, verbose traces for 7
Basic / Auxiliary log tiers Much cheaper ingestion for high-volume, rarely-queried tables (with query limitations) 🔄
Commitment tiers Discount at 100 GB/day and above
Daily cap ⚠️ A safety net — but it stops ingestion when hit, blinding you. Alert before the cap
Fix the chatty source ⭐ Review the top 10 log sources by volume quarterly — there's always one line producing 60% of the data 
// Where is the money going?
Usage
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) and IsBillable
| summarize GB = round(sum(Quantity) / 1000, 2) by DataType
| order by GB desc

// Which operation is generating the most trace volume?
traces
| where timestamp > ago(1d)
| summarize count() by operation_Name, severityLevel
| order by count_ desc

9. Incident response on Azure

1. ASSESS    User impact? How many? Which region/tenant? → Service overview dashboard
2. CHECK     Azure Service Health — is it the platform?
3. WHAT CHANGED?  Activity log + deployment markers + feature flags
4. MITIGATE  Slot swap back · redeploy the previous tag · flag off · scale out · shed load
             ← BEFORE diagnosing. Users don't care about root cause.
5. DIAGNOSE  Metrics → traces → logs for the correlation id → profiler/snapshot
6. VERIFY    Watch the SLO recover
7. POSTMORTEM  Blameless, within 5 days, actions with owners and dates

The Azure-specific diagnostic tools worth knowing:

Tool Use
Activity log ⭐ Who changed what, when. First stop for "it broke and nobody deployed"
Service Health Platform incidents and planned maintenance
App Service → Diagnose and solve problems Automated detectors for restarts, high CPU/memory, failed requests
Application Insights Profiler Sampled CPU traces from production
Snapshot Debugger Captures variable state at the point an exception was thrown
Live Metrics Real-time, unsampled, during a deploy or incident
Kudu (<app>.scm.azurewebsites.net) Files, environment, process explorer, memory dumps

10. Checklist

  • Workspace-based Application Insights on every service, using the connection string
  • One Log Analytics workspace per environment; diagnostic settings on every resource
  • cloud_RoleName set per service so the Application Map is correct
  • Structured logging with named placeholders; correlation id on every entry
  • Trace context propagated across queues, not just HTTP
  • No secrets or PII in telemetry; SQL statement capture reviewed
  • Sampling configured deliberately; exceptions excluded from sampling
  • Service, business, and deep-dive dashboards, with deployment markers
  • Alerts on symptoms with burn-rate windows; each has a runbook and an owner
  • DLQ depth, queue age, certificate expiry, and Key Vault 403/429 alerts
  • Availability tests from ≥3 regions
  • Service Health alerts configured
  • Retention and sampling tuned; ingestion cost reviewed monthly
  • Runbook for the top five alerts; incident process agreed before you need it

🔍 Questions to test yourself

  • Monitoring vs observability? Predefined questions on predefined signals vs enough high-cardinality context to answer new questions without shipping code.
  • Why not alert on CPU? It's a cause, not a symptom. Alert on user-facing SLIs and error-budget burn rate.
  • Why percentiles rather than averages? Users experience the tail. And a dependency's p99 becomes the common case for a request that fans out to it many times.
  • How do you debug a latency regression in Azure? Metrics to scope it → Activity log and deployment markers for what changed → Application Insights traces to find the slow span → logs for that operation_Id → Profiler if it's CPU.
  • Why does telemetry go missing under load? Adaptive sampling. Configure it deliberately and exclude what you must never lose.
  • How do you control Application Insights cost? Sampling, per-table retention, cheaper log tiers for high-volume tables, and — most effectively — fixing the one chatty log line producing most of the volume.
